sections.h2: Where is Chelsea, Massachusetts, and why is it so dense?
sections.html:
Chelsea is a city in Suffolk County on a small peninsula in Boston Harbor, linked to Boston by the Tobin Bridge. At 2.21 square miles of land it is the smallest city in Massachusetts, and the 2020 census counted 40,787 people, which makes it one of the densest places in the state.

Water borders it on three sides. The Island End River separates Chelsea from Everett to the west, the Mystic River and Chelsea Creek form the boundary with Boston to the south and east, and Mill Creek marks part of the border with Revere. Wikipedia lists the elevation at 9.8 feet, with a few small hills rising above the flat ground.

The hills are Admirals Hill, Mount Bellingham, Powderhorn Hill, Mount Washington and Mill Hill. They help divide the city into distinct neighborhoods.

Chelsea has several named areas, each with its own housing mix. These come from Wikipedia's description.

  • Admirals Hill holds the Naval Hospital Historic District and Mary O'Malley Park, the city's largest park.
  • Addison-Orange is flat, residential and densely populated.
  • Bellingham Square became the center of commerce and government after the 1908 fire and includes City Hall and the public library.
  • The Box District, named for early box factories, was rezoned for residential use in the 2000s.
  • Carter Park and Wyndham are a small enclave of mostly single-family Queen Anne homes.
  • Mill Hill has mostly two- and three-story wood-frame detached buildings.
  • Prattville is the northwestern section, and Soldiers Home covers Powderhorn Hill.

If your house is in one of these areas, say so when you talk to a buyer. A single-family house in Carter Park sells to a different buyer than a three-decker in Mill Hill.

sections.h2: What happened in the Great Chelsea Fires?
sections.html:
Chelsea has burned twice on a large scale, and both fires shaped the housing. On April 12, 1908, nearly half the city was destroyed and 18,000 people, 56 percent of the population, lost their homes. The city took about two and a half years to rebuild and was redesigned with wider streets and better emergency access.

In 1973 a second fire destroyed 18 city blocks and affected nearly one-fifth of the city. It started in the rag shop district, where many small businesses handled scrap materials, and spread through wood-frame, closely spaced multifamily buildings.

Wikipedia describes Chelsea's housing as dense, with many wood-frame multifamily buildings. The Department of Fire Services requires a smoke and carbon monoxide certificate for the sale of a home, so fire safety is part of the paperwork whatever the building type.

Among occupied homes, 28 percent of households are one person living alone, and the median age is 33.3 years. Wikipedia reports that 65.8 percent of residents are Hispanic or Latino, and the city has run a Sanctuary City Resolution since 2007.

The city government is the largest employer, and the Massachusetts Water Resources Authority is second. Wikipedia cites the city's 2024 Annual Comprehensive Financial Report for this list.

  • City of Chelsea: 1,650 employees
  • Massachusetts Water Resources Authority: 1,205
  • Massachusetts Information Technology Center: 1,000
  • North Suffolk Mental Health, Chelsea Jewish Healthcare and DiMare Brother: 500 to 999 each
  • Kayem Foods, Metropolitan Credit Union, Delta Management Services and Soldiers Home: 250 to 499 each

Most of the waterfront from the Tobin Bridge to the mouth of Mill Creek is a designated port area, and waterfront use remains primarily industrial.

sections.h2: How did Chelsea's government and history develop?
sections.html:
Samuel Maverick built a palisaded trading post at Winnisimmet in 1624, which is considered the first permanent settlement in Boston Harbor. Chelsea was incorporated as a town in 1739 and became a city in 1857. The Battle of Chelsea Creek in 1775 was the second battle of the American Revolution.

In 1991 Massachusetts placed Chelsea under receivership after a budget deficit of about $9.5 million against a $40 million budget. Voters approved a new charter on June 21, 1994, which replaced the mayor and aldermen with a council-manager system, and local control returned in 1995 when the deficit was gone and the bond rating reached triple-A.

Today an 11-member city council, with three at-large and eight district councilors, works with a city manager. Public schools include four elementary schools, three middle schools and Chelsea High School, plus Excel Academy and Phoenix Charter Academy as public charters. Bunker Hill Community College has a satellite location in the city.

sections.h2: How do you get around Chelsea?
sections.html:
The MBTA Silver Line SL3 has served the city since 2018, running from South Station to four Chelsea stops: Eastern Avenue, Box District, Downtown Chelsea and Mystic Mall.

A commuter rail station on the Newburyport/Rockport Line connects to North Station, and several MBTA bus routes link to East Boston, Revere and Everett. Route 1 is a limited-access highway that cuts the city in half, and the Tobin Bridge carries it to Charlestown.

The Silver Line also connects to Logan Airport and to the Blue Line at Airport Station. The Box District and Downtown Chelsea stations are the ones nearest the city center.

sections.h2: How do Chelsea's tax rates and assessments work?
sections.html:
Chelsea's Assessing Department values every property in the city and administers residential and statutory exemptions. For fiscal year 2026 the residential rate is $11.48 per $1,000 and the commercial, industrial and personal property rate is $23.79 per $1,000.

The city also has a residential exemption worth $3,203.68 in tax dollars, which equals $279,066 in assessed value. Ask the assessors whether your home qualifies. The office is in Room 211 at City Hall, 500 Broadway, and the phone is 617-466-4010. Hours are Monday to Thursday, 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., Tuesday evening from 4 to 7 p.m., and Friday morning until noon.

We did not find a Chelsea page with confirmed bill due dates, so check your bill or call the office. See the Assessor page for forms and the property record cards.

sections.h2: What should a Chelsea seller prepare before closing?
sections.html:
Massachusetts sets the deed excise tax at $2.00 per $500 of price or fraction of $500 under MGL c. 64D, s. 1. The registry of deeds for the county collects it at recording, and the Assessor page links to the Suffolk County Registry of Deeds.

  • Schedule the smoke and carbon monoxide inspection with the Chelsea Fire Department once you have a closing date.
  • Pull the deed, tax bill and any permit records.
  • If tenants live there, gather leases and note rents.
  • If the house is inherited, ask the probate court or an attorney what is needed first.

If you would rather skip showings and repairs, Cash Home Buyers can look at a Chelsea house as it stands and give you a written offer to compare with a listing.

faqs.q: What county is Chelsea, MA in?
faqs.a: Chelsea is in Suffolk County, the same county as Boston. It sits across the Mystic River from Charlestown.

faqs.q: Is Chelsea the smallest city in Massachusetts?
faqs.a: Yes. At about 2.2 square miles of land, Chelsea is the smallest city in the state by land area.

faqs.q: What was the Great Chelsea Fire?
faqs.a: On April 12, 1908, a fire destroyed nearly half the city and left 18,000 people homeless. A second fire in 1973 destroyed 18 city blocks.

faqs.q: What is Chelsea's residential tax rate?
faqs.a: For fiscal year 2026 the residential rate is $11.48 per $1,000 of assessed value. The commercial, industrial and personal property rate is $23.79.

faqs.q: Does Chelsea have a residential exemption?
faqs.a: Yes. The Assessor lists a residential exemption of $3,203.68 in tax dollars for fiscal year 2026, equal to $279,066 in assessed value.

faqs.q: Do I need a smoke and CO certificate to sell in Chelsea?
faqs.a: Yes. Massachusetts requires a certificate of compliance from the local fire department for a home sale or transfer.
